actions.justification: ★ MANDATORY: Patient has hypertension and diabetes, both major AKI risk factors. Must identify all contributing risk factors as first step per KDIGO AKI guidelines.
★ MANDATORY: Chief complaint is decreased urine output. Urine output monitoring is essential for AKI diagnosis (oliguria <0.5 mL/kg/h) and staging per KDIGO guidelines.
★ MANDATORY: Serum creatinine is required to diagnose and stage AKI per KDIGO criteria (rise ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48h or ≥1.5x baseline within 7 days).
Reassess vital signs to establish baseline and monitor for hemodynamic changes associated with AKI in this hypertensive diabetic patient with decreased urine output.
Evaluate volume status to differentiate prerenal from intrinsic or postrenal AKI, which is critical for determining appropriate management strategy.
Stage the AKI severity using KDIGO criteria based on creatinine (already ordered) to guide intensity of monitoring and treatment decisions.

Calculate eGFR to assess baseline kidney function and severity of AKI in this patient with hypertension and diabetes who presents with decreased urine output. Essential for staging and guiding management.

Review current medications for nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast agents, ACE inhibitors/ARBs) that may be contributing to AKI in this diabetic hypertensive patient. Medication review is a critical early step in AKI workup.

Assess contrast-induced AKI risk given the patient has diabetes and hypertension — both major risk factors — and decreased urine output suggesting possible pre-existing kidney compromise before any imaging decisions are made.

Patient with decreased urine output and pending creatinine/labs suggesting AKI requires nephrology consultation for expert guidance on management, especially given comorbidities of hypertension and diabetes.

Patients with AKI should have nephrotoxic medications (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, certain antihypertensives, metformin in diabetics) discontinued or held to prevent further renal injury per KDIGO guidelines.
Patient with suspected AKI and high-risk comorbidities (diabetes, hypertension) should avoid iodinated contrast agents to prevent contrast-induced AKI per KDIGO contrast-AKI guidelines.

Patient with AKI (decreased urine output, pending creatinine) is at risk for hyperkalemia. ECG should be performed to assess for peaked T-waves or other hyperkalemic changes, which is a critical safety check in AKI management.

Patient has hypertension and diabetes - both major risk factors for CKD. Assessing for underlying or evolving CKD is important to differentiate AKI from CKD or AKI-on-CKD, which impacts prognosis and management.
With decreased urine output and pending labs, early assessment of renal replacement therapy need is appropriate to ensure timely planning if oliguria worsens or metabolic derangements emerge.
Given persistent AKI with decreased urine output, hypertension, and diabetes as comorbidities, nephrology follow-up is warranted to guide further management even though initial consult was done.
With AKI and decreased urine output, it is important to formally evaluate indications for renal replacement therapy (uremia, refractory hyperkalemia, fluid overload, acidosis).
Ensure all nephrotoxic medications (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast agents, etc.) are discontinued to prevent further renal injury in this AKI patient with diabetes and hypertension.
NSAIDs are nephrotoxic and should be held in AKI to prevent further renal injury, especially in a patient with hypertension and diabetes who already has decreased urine output.
Metformin should be held in AKI due to risk of lactic acidosis, particularly important in this diabetic patient with decreased urine output and pending creatinine.
Assessing vascular access is important for potential IV fluid administration and any future interventions including RRT if needed in this AKI patient.

Patient has AKI (decreased urine output) with pending creatinine. Identifying the etiology (pre-renal, intrinsic renal, post-renal) is a critical next step per KDIGO guidelines, especially given comorbidities of hypertension and diabetes which predispose to both CKD and AKI.

If pre-renal AKI is suspected (decreased urine output, stable hemodynamics), a cautious fluid challenge with isotonic crystalloid is appropriate per KDIGO guidelines to restore renal perfusion, unless contraindicated (e.g., volume overload).

Although RRT is not immediately indicated, early planning is prudent given pending labs, AKI presentation, and comorbidities (diabetes, hypertension). This ensures timely escalation if labs return with severe AKI criteria.
